turns.question: My welder just stopped mid-weld and the screen shows a warning. What happened and what should I do?
turns.answer:
It most likely overheated and shut itself down to protect itself. The warning screen is on the picture below (manual p.23).

The screen lists three possible faults. Read it to see which one you have:

- **Duty Cycle Exceeded:** The machine has thermally tripped. Remedy: let it cool.
- **Low Voltage Input:** The input voltage is below the specified limit. Remedy: check that your input voltage is within the machine's limits.
- **High Voltage Input:** The input voltage is above the specified limit. Remedy: same check.

**What to do**
1. Set the gun (or torch or electrode holder) on a heat-proof surface that doesn't conduct electricity, like a concrete slab. Keep it well away from the ground clamp (manual p.23).
2. **Leave the Power Switch ON.** The internal fan then helps cool the welder (manual p.23).
3. Wait. The welder returns to service on its own once it cools (manual p.23).
4. When it restarts, use shorter welding periods and longer rests (manual p.23).

**Duty cycle** is how many minutes out of 10 you can weld at a given current before the machine needs a rest. For MIG and flux-cored, the manual's rated points are 40% at 100A on 120V and 25% at 200A on 240V (manual p.19). If you weld longer than that, it shuts down.

If the screen says low or high voltage, the machine says to check your input voltage. The manual says no extension cord may be used on this welder (manual p.6). For other power problems, press the Reset Button on the back of the machine (manual p.43).

Which process were you using, and on 120V or 240V? I can give you the exact duty cycle for your setup.

turns.question: I've been running gasless flux-cored wire and now I'm switching to solid wire with shielding gas. What do I need to change?
turns.answer:
Five things change when you go from gasless flux-cored to solid wire with gas. See the diagram and gas photo below.

**First, turn the Power Switch OFF and unplug the welder** before you touch any cables (manual p.10).

1. **Swap the polarity.** Solid wire uses DCEP (electrode positive, meaning the wire is on the positive side). The cable positions reverse from your flux-cored setup (manual p.14):
   - Ground Clamp Cable goes in the **Negative (–)** socket.
   - Wire Feed Power Cable goes in the **Positive (+)** socket.
   - Twist both clockwise all the way to lock them.
2. **Change the feed roller.** Flux-cored uses the knurled groove. Solid wire needs the V-groove roller, turned so the number showing matches your wire diameter (manual p.12).
3. **Raise the feed tension.** Solid wire runs at 3–5. Flux-cored was 2–3 (manual p.15).
4. **Swap the contact tip if needed.** It must match the wire you're using (manual p.17).
5. **Hook up the gas.**
   - Secure the cylinder with two straps.
   - Stand to the side and open the valve briefly to blow out dust, then close it.
   - Thread on the regulator. A C100 cylinder needs the enclosed CGA 580/320 adapter.
   - Connect the gas hose from the regulator to the welder's gas inlet (manual p.14).
   - Check that the gun cable connector is fully inserted, or the gas will leak at the connection (manual p.13).

**DANGER:** Don't open the gas without proper ventilation. Fix leaks immediately. Shielding gas can displace air and cause rapid loss of consciousness and death (manual p.21).

When you power up:
1. Open the cylinder valve all the way.
2. Set the flow gauge to the SCFH on the Settings Chart. The LCD screen says to use 20–30 SCFH (manual p.20, p.21).
3. Pick your gas type from the Settings Chart inside the door. Also check the top of the welder, because p.26 says it's there.
4. Re-enter your wire diameter and material thickness on the LCD (Left Knob and Right Knob).

**Technique also changes.** Tilt the gun from straight on to 15° away from the direction you're welding (push angle). Flux-cored used straight on to 15° in the direction of travel (drag angle) (manual p.22). Keep CTWD (tip-to-work distance) at 1/2" or less.

**Cleanup:** gas-shielded MIG welds don't leave slag, so you won't need to chip (manual p.36).

I can put together a full setup sheet for your job if you tell me the material, thickness, wire size, and whether you're on 120V or 240V.

turns.question: Explain DCEP and DCEN and tell me which process on this machine uses which.
turns.answer:
**DCEP and DCEN are the two ways the welding current can flow.** The "electrode" is the wire, rod or tungsten that carries the arc.

- **DCEP (Direct Current Electrode Positive):** the electrode is wired to the positive (+) socket.
- **DCEN (Direct Current Electrode Negative):** the electrode is wired to the negative (–) socket.

**Which process uses which (manual p.13, 14, 24, 27):**

| Process | Ground clamp | Electrode cable | Polarity |
|---|---|---|---|
| MIG (solid wire, gas) | Negative (–) | Wire Feed Power Cable in Positive (+) | **DCEP** |
| Flux-cored (gasless) | Positive (+) | Wire Feed Power Cable in Negative (–) | **DCEN** |
| TIG | Positive (+) | TIG Torch Cable in Negative (–) | Not labeled in the manual |
| Stick | Negative (–) | Electrode Holder Cable in Positive (+) | Not labeled in the manual |

- TIG would be electrode negative, because the torch is in the negative socket.
- Stick would be electrode positive, because the holder is in the positive socket.

- The plug fits the socket in one orientation only.
- It stays in the same place for every wire process. The polarity swap doesn't affect it.

turns.question: What tension should I set on the feed tensioner?
turns.answer:
Set the Feed Tensioner to **3–5 for solid wire** or **2–3 for flux-cored wire** (manual p.15). The picture below shows the tensioner and idler arm.

Too much force on flux-cored wire will crush it and can cause feeding problems (manual p.15).

Then check the tension with this test (manual p.17):

1. Turn the Power Switch OFF and unplug the welder before you touch the tensioner.
2. Hold the gun 2 to 3 inches from a piece of wood and press the trigger. Keep it under 3 seconds, because the wire stops feeding after 3 seconds if there is no arc.
3. If the wire stops, unplug the welder, tighten the tensioner slightly clockwise, and try again.
4. If the wire bends from the feed pressure, the tension is set properly.

**DANGER** (manual p.16): parts may be at welding voltage. Keep your hands away from the wire feed mechanism, and don't touch the trigger while you feed wire through to the gun.

turns.question: The wire stops feeding while I'm welding, and the spool isn't turning. What should I check?
turns.answer:
Turn the Power Switch OFF and unplug the welder first. The manual says to shut off, disconnect from power, and discharge the MIG gun to ground before you adjust or clean anything (manual p.42).

Check these first, in this order. The flowcharts below show the full lists.

1. **Gun cable bend.** A severely bent cable can stop the feed mechanism from pushing wire. Lay the cable out straight (manual p.42).
2. **Feed roller groove.** Make sure the roller groove matches your wire diameter and wire type. Solid wire uses the V-groove and flux-cored uses the knurled groove (manual p.12, p.42).
3. **Tension.** The manual says to set it to 3–5 for solid wire and 2–3 for flux-cored. Too much force crushes flux-cored wire (manual p.15, p.42).
4. **Liner.** Look for a clogged or worn gun liner, or one that is too small for your wire (manual p.42).
5. **Spool.** Look for wire that is tangled or cross-wound on the spool (manual p.42).

Your spool isn't turning, so the wire is probably not feeding at all. The manual's fix for that case is the tension check in step 27 (manual p.17):

1. Point the gun at a piece of wood 2 to 3 inches away.
2. Press the trigger for less than 3 seconds.
3. If the wire stops instead of bending, unplug the welder and tighten the Feed Tensioner slightly clockwise.
4. Try again until the wire bends.

If the wire feeds but the motor just runs, a Feed Tensioner that is too tight can also cause it. In that case, loosen it (manual p.42).

If the gun, cable or liner looks damaged, the manual says a qualified technician should inspect and replace the parts (manual p.42).

turns.question: How do I load a 10-12 lb spool of wire?
turns.answer:
Here are the steps for a 10-12 lb spool (manual p.10-11). The pictures below show them.

**WARNING:** Turn the Power Switch OFF and unplug the welder first (manual p.10).

1. Pull up on the Door Latch and open the door (p.10).
2. Remove the Wingnut and Spacer. If you're replacing a spool, take off the old spool and pull all the leftover wire out of the liners (p.11).
3. Put the Spool Adapter on the Spool Spindle, against the Spool Brake Pad (p.11).
4. Put the new spool over the adapter. Line up the pin on the adapter with the hole in the spool (p.11).
5. Check the direction. The spool must unwind **clockwise**, or you'll get wire feed problems (p.11).
6. Put the Spacer back on the spindle and secure it with the Wingnut (p.11).
7. Screw the Spool Knob into the Spool Adapter (p.11).
8. Turn the Feed Tensioner knob counterclockwise, just enough to pull it down. This removes the tension, and the spring-loaded Idler Arm moves up (p.11).

**NOTICE:** If the spool spins freely, the Wingnut is too loose. The wire can then unravel and tangle (p.11).

Next, you feed the wire into the liner. Hold the wire end firmly the whole time, or it will unspool (p.15). I can walk you through that part if you'd like.

turns.question: My wire keeps making a bird's nest at the feed rollers. Why?
turns.answer:
A bird's nest is a tangle of wire at the feed rollers. The manual lists four causes (manual p.42). The first three are the most likely, so check them in this order.

**Turn the Power Switch OFF and unplug the welder before you adjust anything.** Also discharge the MIG gun to ground (manual p.42).

1. **Too much wire feed pressure.** This is the first cause the manual lists. Re-set the Feed Tensioner using the test in step 27 (manual p.17). Feed the wire against a piece of wood 2–3 inches away. If the wire stops, tighten the tensioner a little. If the wire bends, the tension is right. The manual says tension should be 3–5 for solid wire and 2–3 for flux-cored wire (manual p.15). Too much force on flux-cored wire crushes it and can cause feeding problems.
2. **Wrong contact tip size.** Replace it with the right tip for your wire (manual p.42).
3. **Gun cable connector not fully seated.** Push the connector fully into the socket on the wire feed mechanism, then tighten the knob. Don't overtighten it (manual p.13).
4. **Damaged liner.** Have a qualified technician inspect it and repair or replace it if needed (manual p.42).

The flowchart below has the full list. Gasless flux-cored wire uses no shielding gas, so none of these causes are gas-related.

turns.question: Walk me through feeding the wire for the first time without welding.
turns.answer:
You feed the wire with the Cold Wire Feed Switch, so you never pull the trigger. This assumes the spool is already on and the gun cable is connected (manual p.10–13). The pictures below show the hold-the-wire step and the cold feed step.

**DANGER (manual p.16):** Parts may be at welding voltage. Keep your hands away from the wire feed mechanism. Close the door before plugging in, unless you are using Cold Wire Feed. Do not touch the trigger while feeding wire to the gun.

1. Turn the Power Switch OFF and unplug the welder (manual p.10).
2. Hold the end of the wire firmly and keep tension on it for the next steps. If you let go, the wire unravels and tangles (manual p.15).
3. Cut off any bent or crimped wire. The cut end should have no burrs or sharp edges (manual p.15).
4. Guide at least 12 inches of wire into the Wire Inlet Liner and Feed Guide (manual p.15).
5. Seat the wire in the groove of the Feed Roller. Push the Idler Arm down. Swing the Feed Tensioner up to latch across the arm tip. Then you can let go of the wire (manual p.15).
6. Set the tension. The manual says 3–5 for solid wire and 2–3 for flux-cored. Too much force crushes flux-cored wire (manual p.15).
7. Pull the nozzle off. Unscrew the contact tip counterclockwise and remove it (manual p.15).
8. Lay the gun cable out in a straight line. Keep it very straight for stainless wire (manual p.15).
9. Plug in and turn the Power Switch ON (manual p.16). Do not touch the trigger.
10. Point the gun away from everything. Press and hold the Cold Wire Feed Switch until about 2 inches of wire comes out (manual p.16).

- **Liner pops out with the wire:** This is normal. Push it back into the gun (manual p.16).
- **Wire won't feed and the spool isn't turning:** Turn OFF and unplug. Tighten the Feed Tensioner slightly clockwise, then try again (manual p.16).

**Next:** Test the tension by feeding wire against a piece of wood 2–3 inches away. Do this for less than 3 seconds. Tighten a little at a time until the wire bends instead of stopping (manual p.17). Then turn OFF and unplug. Fit a contact tip that matches your wire, put the nozzle back, and trim the wire to 1/2" stickout (manual p.17).

turns.question: What's CTWD and what gun angle should I use for flux-cored versus solid wire?
turns.answer:
**CTWD** means Contact Tip to Work Distance. It's how far the tip of the gun's contact tip sits from the metal. Keep the tip within 1/2" of the work surface (manual p.22). The diagnosis pages also say to keep CTWD under 1/2" (manual p.35). A CTWD that is too long can cause porosity, spatter and a wavy bead (manual p.37).

**Gun angle** (manual p.22, quoted exactly):

- **Solid wire with shielding gas (MIG):** the wire is "angled anywhere in-between straight on and 15° away from the direction you are welding." The manual calls this the **push angle**.
- **Flux-cored wire without gas:** the wire is "angled anywhere in-between straight on and 15° in the direction you are welding." The manual calls this the **drag angle**.

The picture below shows both angles and the CTWD.

The manual also gives the angle into the joint (p.22). Aim the wire straight into the joint. That is 90° for a butt weld and 45° for a fillet (T-shaped) weld.

turns.question: How do I pick MIG on the screen and set wire size and thickness?
turns.answer:
Here are the steps (manual p.20). The pictures below show the knobs and the LCD screen.

1. Turn the Power Switch ON.
2. Press the **Home** button.
3. Turn the **Main Control Knob** until MIG appears on the screen.
4. Press the Main Control Knob to select it.
5. Follow the polarity and gas screen. Plug the cables in as it shows, and connect the gas. Set the flow between 20 and 30 SCFH (cubic feet per hour of gas). Press the Main Control Knob to go to the next screen.

If you're using gasless flux-cored wire, the same steps apply. You just skip the gas.

turns.question: Walk me through setting up stick welding on the screen, and what are Hot Start and Arc Force?
turns.answer:
**Stick setup on the screen (manual p.32)**

First, turn the Power Switch OFF and unplug the welder before you touch any cables. Then plug in the cables (manual p.27). The diagram below shows it:
- Ground Clamp Cable goes in the **Negative (–)** socket.
- Electrode Holder Cable goes in the **Positive (+)** socket.
- No shielding gas is needed.

Then do the LCD steps:
1. Plug the welder into a grounded, GFCI-protected outlet, with the Power Switch OFF. Set the electrode holder down on a non-conductive, non-flammable surface, away from grounded objects. Turn the Power Switch ON.
2. Press **Home**. Turn the **Main Control Knob** until Stick appears, then press it to select.
3. **Polarity screen:** plug the cables in as the screen shows. Press the Main Control Knob to go to the next screen. (Back returns to the previous one.)
4. **Electrode type:** turn the Main Control Knob. The example screen shows 60xx.
5. **Diameter and thickness:** Left Knob sets electrode diameter. Right Knob sets material thickness.
6. **Auto Weld screen:** Left Knob sets amperage. Turn the Right Knob to ON to energize the electrode holder.

WARNING (manual p.32): once the Right Knob is ON, the welder is energized and open circuit voltage is present. Open circuit voltage (OCV) is the voltage at the electrode before you strike an arc.

**Hot Start and Arc Force** (Optional Settings, manual p.33)

To reach them, press the Main Control Knob to enter Optional Settings. Turn the knob to pick one, press to select it, then turn to adjust.
- **Hot Start:** adjusts the amperage at the start of the weld.
- **Arc Force:** adjusts weld penetration and smoothness.

The manual doesn't give numbers for either. It also says the initial settings may need adjusting after you stop and inspect the weld (manual p.33). The same menu has Recall Setting and Save Setting, which holds up to 5 configurations.

turns.question: What wire speed and voltage should I use for 1/8 inch mild steel with 0.030 flux-cored wire?
turns.answer:
The manual doesn't give a wire speed or voltage number for this job, so I won't guess one. The welder picks them for you. 1/8" steel is inside the chart's flux-cored range (18 gauge to 5/16"), and 0.030" is a size the welder takes for flux-cored wire (manual p.7).

**How to get the settings (manual p.20):**
1. Turn the Left Knob to set wire diameter: 0.030".
2. Turn the Right Knob to set material thickness: 1/8".
3. On the Auto Weld screen, the Left Knob adjusts wire feed speed (amperage) and the Right Knob adjusts voltage. The white mark on the line shows the recommended setting. See the LCD picture below.

The Settings Chart inside the door has settings too, but it isn't reproduced in the manual. Look inside the door first, then on top of the welder, because the manual disagrees on where it is (p.14, p.30 versus p.26).

**Also set up (manual p.13, p.15):**
- Turn the Power Switch OFF and unplug the welder before moving any cable. Ground Clamp Cable goes in the Positive (+) socket and Wire Feed Power Cable in the Negative (–) socket. This is DCEN (electrode negative). No gas is needed. See the diagram below.
- Feed roller: the knurled (flux-cored) groove for 0.030".
- Feed tension: 2–3. Too much crushes flux-cored wire.
- Keep the tip within 1/2" of the work (CTWD, the contact tip to work distance).

**Current limits depend on your outlet.** The chart doesn't say which voltage the 1/8" job needs.
- 120V: 30–140 A. Rated 40% at 100 A, or 100% continuous at 75 A.
- 240V: 30–220 A. Rated 25% at 200 A, or 100% continuous at 115 A.

On 120V the chart allows 1/8" on paper, but the manual doesn't confirm the job is achievable there. 240V gives more current range (general advice).

The manual says the initial settings may need adjusting after you stop and inspect the weld (p.21). Practicing on scrap of the same thickness first is also general advice. The full sheet is below.
